identity.title: Physics
identity.subtitle: Physics builds models of the physical world. Begin with the regime that matches the system: familiar macroscopic conditions, or the high-speed, strong-gravity, atomic, and subatomic regimes where classical assumptions stop working.

groups.label: Classical Physics
groups.condition: Best fit: ordinary speeds, macroscopic scales, and weak gravity.
groups.description: Classical models describe most everyday systems extremely well. They treat motion, fields, waves, and bulk matter with continuous quantities and deterministic laws.

items.label: Mechanics
items.summary: Describe motion, identify interactions, and track energy and momentum through physical systems.

items.label: Waves & Optics
items.summary: Study oscillation, propagation, interference, sound, light, reflection, refraction, and imaging.

items.label: Thermodynamics
items.summary: Connect microscopic motion to temperature, heat, internal energy, entropy, and macroscopic change.

items.label: Electromagnetism
items.summary: Model charge, electric and magnetic fields, circuits, induction, and electromagnetic radiation.

groups.label: Modern Physics
groups.condition: Required for near-light speed, strong gravity, and atomic or subatomic scales.
groups.description: Modern physics extends the classical picture when its assumptions fail. Relativity changes spacetime; quantum theory changes how physical states and measurements behave.

items.label: Relativity
items.summary: Rebuild space, time, motion, and gravity when speed or gravitational curvature becomes significant.

items.label: Quantum Physics
items.summary: Describe states, amplitudes, quantization, uncertainty, measurement, and nonclassical behavior.

items.label: Atomic Physics
items.summary: Apply quantum theory to electron structure, spectra, energy levels, transitions, and atom-light interactions.

items.label: Nuclear Physics
items.summary: Study nuclei, binding energy, radioactivity, fission, fusion, and nuclear reactions.

sections.title: The conditions tell you which theory to use.
sections.summary: A newer theory does not make an older one useless. It explains where the older model works, and what must change outside that range.

choices.question: Are speeds far below light speed and gravity relatively weak?
choices.detail: Mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, and waves cover most human-scale phenomena.

choices.question: Are speeds close to light speed, or is gravity strongly curving spacetime?
choices.detail: Special relativity handles inertial high-speed motion; general relativity handles gravity as geometry.

choices.question: Does the system depend on atoms, nuclei, photons, or quantized states?
choices.detail: Atomic and nuclear physics apply quantum rules to particular kinds of matter and interaction.
